title: Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff
summary: The container starts, exits, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with growing delay.

steps.title: Confirm it is actually looping
steps.look: RESTARTS climbing over successive checks. A high but static count is an old incident, not a live one.

signals.means: This is a Job or a one-shot container that finished. restartPolicy is wrong, not the app.

steps.title: Read the previous container's logs
steps.look: The FIRST fatal line, not the last. Startup errors scroll off the top and the tail is usually just the shutdown noise.

signals.means: It died waiting on a dependency that was not reachable.
Required configuration was absent at startup.
The process cannot read a path or bind a port as its runAsUser.

steps.title: Read the termination state
steps.look: exitCode and reason. This is the single most decisive field in the whole runbook.

signals.means: The kernel killed it for memory. No amount of restarting will fix this.
The entrypoint was found but is not executable. Check the file mode in the image.
The entrypoint was not found at all. Wrong path, or missing shell in a distroless base.
The application chose to exit. The reason is in the logs, not here.

steps.title: Check whether a probe is doing the killing
steps.look: Events for 'Liveness probe failed'. If present, the app may be healthy but slow to start, and the probe is executing it.

signals.means: The liveness probe is killing a container that may only need more startup time.

causes.cause: A required env var, Secret key or ConfigMap key is absent, so the process exits during startup.
causes.fix: Fix the owning Deployment/Secret/ConfigMap in source control and reconcile. Do not patch the live Pod.

causes.cause: The container's memory limit is below its real working set.
causes.fix: Raise limits.memory in the owning Deployment, or fix the leak. Restarting will reproduce it every time.

causes.cause: A database, cache or upstream service was not reachable at startup.
causes.fix: Confirm the dependency's Service has endpoints, then decide whether the app should retry instead of exiting.

causes.cause: initialDelaySeconds is shorter than the app's real startup time, so liveness kills it mid-boot.
causes.fix: Move the slow-start allowance to a startupProbe rather than inflating the liveness delay.

causes.cause: Exit 127. The command in the image manifest does not exist at that path.
causes.fix: Check the Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT/CMD against the built image. A distroless base has no /bin/sh.

causes.cause: Exit 126. The file exists but lacks the execute bit, or its interpreter line is wrong.
causes.fix: Add chmod +x in the Dockerfile, or fix the shebang. Rebuild the image.

causes.cause: runAsUser cannot read a mounted path or bind a privileged port.
causes.fix: Correct fsGroup on the volume, or move the app to a port above 1024.

causes.cause: A one-shot workload is running under restartPolicy Always.
causes.fix: Run it as a Job with restartPolicy OnFailure or Never.

verify: RESTARTS holds steady across at least three checks spanning the app's normal startup window.
The container reports Ready, and readiness has not flapped in recent events.
The original failing request or job path completes successfully.
escalate: Image tag and digest, plus resources and probe definitions

title: Pod stays Pending and is never scheduled
summary: The Pod object exists but no node has accepted it.

steps.title: Read the scheduler's own reason
steps.look: The scheduler states exactly why each node was rejected, in the form '0/N nodes are available: ...'. Read that string before anything else.

signals.means: No node has enough free allocatable resource for the requests.
The nodeSelector or affinity rule matches no node's labels.
Every candidate node carries a taint this Pod does not tolerate.
This is a storage problem wearing a scheduling costume.

signals.match: (?i)node\(s\) didn't find available persistent volumes|volume node affinity conflict
signals.means: The PV is pinned to a zone the scheduler cannot place the Pod in.

steps.title: Compare the request against real allocatable capacity
steps.look: Requests, not usage. A node at 12% CPU usage can still be 100% requested and therefore unschedulable.

steps.title: Read what this Pod is actually asking for
steps.look: Compare these three against the previous step. The mismatch is usually obvious once both are on screen.

causes.cause: The sum of requests exceeds allocatable on every node.
causes.fix: Lower the request to the workload's real profile, or add capacity. Raising the limit does not help; the scheduler reads requests.

causes.cause: nodeSelector or nodeAffinity references labels no node carries, often after a node pool was replaced.
causes.fix: Correct the selector, or label the intended nodes. Check for typos in the label key first.

causes.cause: Nodes are tainted (NoSchedule) and the Pod has no matching toleration.
causes.fix: Add the toleration if the Pod belongs on those nodes, otherwise target a different pool.

causes.cause: A referenced PVC has not bound, so the Pod cannot be placed.
causes.fix: Follow the PVC Pending runbook. Nothing about the Pod spec will fix this.

causes.cause: An existing PV lives in one zone and the Pod cannot be scheduled there.
causes.fix: Use a topology-aware StorageClass with volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer.

verify: The Pod reports a nodeName and moves past Pending.
No new FailedScheduling events appear for this Pod.
The change was made in the owning manifest, not by editing the live Pod.
escalate: Allocated resources block from describe nodes
The Pod's requests, nodeSelector and tolerations

title: Service exists but returns connection refused
summary: DNS resolves the Service, but nothing answers. Usually the Service has no endpoints.

steps.title: Check whether the Service has any endpoints at all
steps.look: ENDPOINTS column. If it is empty or <none>, the Service is pointing at nothing and the problem is the selector or pod readiness, not the network.

signals.means: No pods are backing this Service.

steps.title: Compare the Service selector against real pod labels
steps.cmd: kubectl get svc {service} -n {namespace} -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}{"\n"}' && kubectl get pods -n {namespace} --show-labels
steps.look: An exact match on every key. One extra or renamed label is enough to produce an empty Service, and this is the most common cause by a wide margin.

signals.means: Compare character by character. 'app' and 'app.kubernetes.io/name' are different keys.

steps.title: Check whether the backing pods are Ready
steps.look: A pod that is Running but 0/1 Ready is excluded from endpoints. Readiness, not liveness, controls Service membership.

signals.means: The pod is up but failing readiness, so it is deliberately kept out of the Service.

steps.title: Confirm the target port matches the container port
steps.look: targetPort must match the container's real listening port, or a named port the container declares. port is what clients dial; targetPort is where it lands.

causes.cause: The Service selector does not match the pod labels.
causes.fix: Align them in the manifests. Changing the Deployment's pod labels forces a rollout, so prefer correcting the Service.

causes.cause: Pods are running but failing their readiness probe, so kube-proxy excludes them.
causes.fix: Fix the readiness endpoint or its threshold. The Service will populate on its own once pods report Ready.

causes.cause: targetPort points at a port nothing is listening on.
causes.fix: Set targetPort to the container's real port, or use a named port so the two cannot drift.

verify: EndpointSlice lists the expected pod IPs.
A request from inside the cluster to the Service name succeeds.
The count of endpoints matches the number of Ready replicas.
